status: draft — confirm with RAB / a postharvest specialist before production
applies_to: Mature or young carrots, tops cut to under 2.5 cm, washed. Held 1–4 weeks before sale.

sources: UC Davis Postharvest Research and Extension Center, Carrot produce fact sheet

why_these_numbers.targetC: 0°C is ideal but the ice water is ~0-1°C, so the chamber can't reach it safely. 2°C is the coldest safe target; quality at 2°C stays good for several weeks, at 4°C it is acceptable, at 6°C and above sprouting, rooting and bitterness come much faster.
why_these_numbers.alarmHighC: Above ~5°C carrots respire faster, lose sweetness and water, and start to root or sprout.
why_these_numbers.freezeGuardC: Carrots freeze at about -1.4°C. The air leaving the coil is the coldest in the room, so cooling stops when THAT air reaches 0°C. Frozen spots thaw into soft, water-soaked patches that rot.
why_these_numbers.rhHigh: Above ~98% with poor hygiene, white mould (Sclerotinia) spreads between crates. 97% stops the humidifier before that.
why_these_numbers.humidityGraceMin: Short humidity dips (door opened, loading) do no harm; carrots wilt only after hours of dry air. A dip counts only after 2 hours.

humidity_method: First choice: plastic crates lined with thin perforated polyethylene bags (about 0.03–0.05 mm, a few small holes per bag). The carrots' own moisture keeps the air in the bag near 95%, with no free water.
Second: a damp layer of clay bricks or gravel on the floor (keep it damp, never pooled). No standing water on the floor.
Ultrasonic humidifiers are off by default: hard water clogs them and can wet the crop.
handling_rules: Get carrots into cold storage within 3 hours of harvest. Keep them in the shade until then.
Sort before storing: remove broken, cracked, forked, insect-damaged or rotting roots.
Cut the tops to under 2.5 cm. Leaves pull water out of the root.
Wash in clean water with 100–150 ppm free chlorine at pH 6.5–7.5 (or a food-grade peracetic acid product). Change the water when it gets dirty.
Pre-cool before loading: rinse in the coldest water available. The cold room holds carrots cold but cannot quickly cool a large warm load.
Do not cure carrots (unlike potatoes and onions). Curing only dries them out.
Use ventilated plastic crates, not sacks or wooden boxes.
Keep crates out of the direct blast of the fan and not touching the radiator.
Clean and disinfect crates and the floor between batches. Drain coil condensate outside the chamber.

storage_diseases.name: Bacterial soft rot (Pectobacterium)
storage_diseases.triggers: Free water on roots, bruising, freeze damage

storage_diseases.name: White mould (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
storage_diseases.signs: White cottony growth with hard black bodies
storage_diseases.triggers: Very high humidity with poor hygiene, infected roots brought in

storage_diseases.name: Black rot (Alternaria radicina)
storage_diseases.signs: Sunken black lesions, often at the crown
storage_diseases.triggers: Field infection, skin damage at harvest or sorting

not_ideal.potato: Not ethylene-producing, but table potatoes turn sweet below ~4°C. Store them in a separate, warmer room.

to_verify: RSB carrot standard number (an AI answer said 'RS 242'; not confirmed). Ask RSB for the current carrot specification.
